body.text: In short:
Bupa is continuing its expansion into general practice by buying up GP clinics, including substantial chains of centres.
A former patient and former receptionist have accused the insurer of neglecting a clinic before shutting it, something Bupa rejects.
What's next?
Bupa's purchase of the Partnered Health chain has been approved by the competition regulator.
Trish Jamieson says it was her close relationship with her GP of 15 years that was instrumental in identifying early she had oesophageal cancer in 2018.
"I went to the doctors, and I saw her on the Friday and she was on the phone to St Vincent's Hospital organising me to go in there on the Monday," she said.
"I got it early enough that hopefully I'm going to get through it."
Her GP was based in Eastbrooke Belrose Family Practice, a clinic in Sydney's north frequented by elderly patients in nearby retirement homes.

Like many of her fellow patients, Ms Jamieson was devastated when health insurance giant Bupa closed down the practice in March, just 15 months after purchasing it as part of a strategy to buy up GP clinics nationally.
Former receptionist Alana Monaci said it was the type of clinic that held 100th birthday parties for lonely patients and whose nurses were always on hand for a cup of tea and a hug.
"Patients were coming in, literally crying in the waiting room,"
Bupa closes several GP clinics
The Belrose clinic was one of three Australian general practices that Bupa bought and subsequently closed.
A nearby Sydney GP clinic in Seaforth was converted into one of Bupa's new Mindplace mental health centres.
A Gold Coast clinic, Eastbrooke Family Clinic Southport, was also closed down in April, shortly after being purchased.

Bupa's Sydney patients were told they could attend the insurer's new larger clinic at Gordon, a tricky journey across town for the elderly that required them to navigate Sydney's congested north shore traffic.
The closure of these small clinics comes as Bupa builds its GP network through acquisitions, as well as expands into psychology services.
Bupa currently operates 33 Bupa Medical and 13 Mindplace clinics but has flagged it wants to operate more.
It follows a similar expansion by rival insurer Medibank Private, which had acquired a majority 90 per cent stake in the MyHealth GP chain by 2024.
Bupa announced in June it intended to buy another 68 clinics from GP chain Partnered Health as part of its push.
The ABC yesterday revealed a Bupa clinic encouraged GPs to maximise Medicare billings in a push to increase revenue.
Bupa accused of letting GP clinic fail
The experience has raised questions about insurers' move into the GP space.
Royal Australian College of GPs (RACGP) president Michael Wright said insurers had a financial interest in keeping people healthy through preventative care.
"High-quality GP care is probably going to decrease the demand on the hospital services, which in the long run might save them some money,"
he said.
But not everyone is convinced.
Ms Monaci said in the 15 months Bupa ran the Belrose clinic, conditions there noticeably declined.
She said the clinic had to wait eight months for an air conditioner to be repaired and it became a lot more difficult to order medical supplies and get IT help.
"Just layers, layers of communication that they had to go through to get really quite simple things," she said.
Ms Jamieson also noticed that when Bupa took over the clinic she attended in 2025 things dramatically changed.
She could no longer get urgent appointments when she experienced side effects from her cancer treatment.
"When Bupa took over, there's no level of care. Not really any level of care at all."
'Unsettling' experience as doors close
When one of the clinic's longstanding GPs decided to retire and another went on parental leave in March, Ms Monaci said Bupa seized the chance to close the practice.
The ABC understands the clinic's location underneath a residential building was problematic and, when it had trouble attracting new GPs, the site was deemed unviable.
"The amount of tears that were shed in that last couple of weeks from everyone [was huge], not just us behind the reception,"
Ms Monaci said.
In a statement, Bupa said the Seaforth Belrose clinic closed after a review of local needs and nearby services, and that staff were offered redeployment opportunities.
The company said it understood "changes to local medical centres can be unsettling to patients and employees".

Bupa said that was why it communicated directly with patients, "established a dedicated hotline to support transfers of care to local GPs" or nearby Bupa medical centres "depending on what best served their needs and preferences".
Corporates continue GP expansion

A Bupa spokesperson said as it expanded, Bupa was improving existing practices and making upgrades, including site refurbishments, service additions, technology improvements, and increased accessibility.
"We opened five new medical centres over the past 12 months and expect our network to continue growing," they said.
"We're expanding our primary care network because we know better health outcomes start with earlier, preventive care and easier access to GPs close to where Australians live and work."

The RACGP's Dr Wright said there was likely to be increasing corporatisation of medical centres because Medicare rebates were failing to keep up with cost-of-living increases, and larger practices could be run more efficiently.
"We just want to make sure we don't get a two-tier system where we kind of get one type of care if you go to a corporate practice and a different type of care at others."
Health economist Terry Barnes said health insurers had more interest in the patients' wellbeing than private equity firms, which own some practices.
"Bupa or any other health insurer in practice ownership needs to actually be a responsible owner."
Bupa said it was expanding its primary care network because "better health outcomes start with earlier, preventive care and easier access to GPs".
But Alana Monaci is concerned with the growing corporatisation of medical practices.
